title: Fielded Max-Sim Keying for Assistant-Side Memory Recall in Long-Term Conversational Assistants

contributions.purpose: Close the retrieval gap for single-session-assistant (SSA) queries, where users ask about information the assistant previously provided, without harming other query types.
contributions.mechanism: Fielded max-sim keying treats each conversation round as a two-field document with separate embeddings for user and assistant content and scores relevance as the maximum similarity across fields; requires no additional training, only a change in indexing/scoring.
contributions.evaluation: On LongMemEval, matches user-only indexing on overall Recall@10 while improving SSA metrics (see C2).
contributions.source_quote: We propose fielded max-sim keying, which treats each conversation round as a two-field document with separate embeddings for user and assistant content, scoring by maximum similarity across fields.

contributions.purpose: Show the method is a risk-free drop-in replacement (zero-harm property).
contributions.mechanism: Compares fielded max-sim against user-only indexing on overall and SSA-specific retrieval metrics.
contributions.evaluation: Identical overall Recall@10 (0.664) to user-only indexing while improving SSA Recall@10 by +0.018 and NDCG@10 by +0.038.
contributions.source_quote: We demonstrate a zero-harm property: fielded max-sim achieves identical overall Recall@10 (0.664) to user-only indexing while improving SSA Recall@10 by +0.018 and NDCG@10 by +0.038, enabling risk-free adoption as a drop-in replacement.

contributions.purpose: Explain why the naive alternative (concatenating user+assistant text) fails.
contributions.mechanism: Empirical measurement of cross-field interference in concatenation-based indexing.
contributions.evaluation: Concatenation degrades overall Recall@10 by -0.145 despite improving SSA recall, evidencing cross-field interference.
contributions.source_quote: We provide empirical evidence of cross-field interference in concatenation-based indexing, which degrades overall Recall@10 by -0.145 despite improving SSA recall, explaining why naive field combination fails.

contributions.purpose: Justify the non-linear max operator over linear score mixing.
contributions.mechanism: Compares max-sim scoring against linear mixture scoring of the two fields.
contributions.evaluation: Only the non-linear max operator achieves zero-harm; linear mixtures trade SSA gains for unacceptable overall degradation.
contributions.source_quote: We compare max-sim against linear mixture scoring and show that only the non-linear max operator achieves zero-harm-linear mixtures trade SSA gains for unacceptable overall degradation.

self_declared_provenance.quote: The method requires no additional training and serves as a drop-in replacement for existing retrieval pipelines.

notes: The bullet 'Our contributions are:' list (page 2) contains only the three demonstration/analysis items (C2-C4); the core method proposal (C1) is stated in intro/abstract prose, not as a bullet. Method's max-sim scoring is lineage of ColBERT late interaction (Related Work 2.3), but that subsection is cut off at the bottom of page 2 with no explicit extend/adapt statement.
